planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sharply drained, acidic, low-phosphorus mountain-fynbos-type soil in full sun with good air movement.

directions: Queen Protea forms a low, often sprawling evergreen shrub prized for some of the largest and most elegant flowerheads in the genus, with broad pink bracts fringed in silvery hair surrounding a cream to pink center, opening mainly in the cooler months. Native to higher-elevation mountain fynbos in South Africa's Cape Floristic Region, it needs the same sharp, nutrient-poor drainage and phosphorus-free regime as other Proteas but tolerates somewhat cooler, moister mountain conditions than coastal species. Site it in full sun with excellent air movement and avoid any winter wet feet, since root rot is the most common killer of container-grown plants. Established plants are usually killed outright by wildfire and regenerate entirely from soil-stored seed, so gardeners should not expect stump resprouting after a hard freeze or burn.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sharply drained, low-phosphorus soil in full sun, giving this taller sugarbush generous room and wind protection while young.

directions: Sugarbush Protea grows into one of the taller, more upright shrubs in the genus, bearing cream to soft-pink flowerheads above narrow gray-green leaves on a plant that can eventually reach small-tree proportions in favorable sites. It shares the genus-wide need for sharp drainage, mineral and acidic low-phosphorus soil, and full sun, and resents heavy clay or routine fertilizer applications. Because of its eventual height, give it generous spacing and wind protection while young, loosely staking the leader until the woody framework sets. Like most sugarbushes it is water-wise and summer-drought-tolerant once established, needing supplemental irrigation only through its first year or two in the ground.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sandy, sharply drained, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; this coastal species tolerates salt wind better than most Proteas.

directions: Saldanha Protea is a dense, rounded coastal shrub from the limestone and sandy fynbos near Saldanha Bay, bearing cream flowerheads tipped in dark maroon-brown that give off a faintly yeasty scent thought to attract beetle pollinators. It tolerates salt-laden coastal wind and sandy soils better than many Protea species but still demands the sharp drainage and phosphorus-free feeding the genus requires everywhere. Grow it in full sun in a Mediterranean-climate garden and avoid overhead irrigation, which encourages the fungal leaf and stem problems this species is prone to in humid conditions. Its compact, wind-firm habit makes it a useful choice for exposed coastal protea plantings where taller species would need staking.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sharply drained, limestone-derived or neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun; more lime-tolerant than most Proteas.

directions: Limestone Sugarbush is native to a narrow band of coastal limestone fynbos along South Africa's southern Cape coast, where it forms a rounded shrub with blunt-tipped leaves and pink-to-cream flowerheads produced over a long autumn-into-winter season. It is naturally adapted to alkaline, free-draining limestone-derived soils, making it more lime-tolerant than most Proteas, which generally insist on acidic conditions. Plant it in full sun with sharp drainage and skip phosphorus fertilizer as with the rest of the genus, but there is no need to acidify the soil for this particular species. Its long cut-flower vase life and reliable cool-season bloom have made it a mainstay of the South African cut-flower trade.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into lean, rocky, acidic, sharply drained soil in full sun; a mountain fynbos species best suited to Mediterranean-climate gardens.

directions: Rose Spoon Protea is a mountain fynbos shrub named for its narrow, spoon-shaped pink bracts tipped with dense silvery wool, opening into tall, pointed flowerheads in the cooler months. Like many high-elevation Protea species it is killed outright by fire and persists only through seed banked in the soil, so it is not a plant to count on resprouting after a hard freeze or burn. Give it full sun, lean rocky or sandy acidic soil with sharp drainage, and a complete absence of phosphorus fertilizer, matching the needs of its genus relatives. It performs best in Mediterranean-climate gardens with cool, moist winters and dry summers, and resents humid, high-rainfall summer climates.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sharply drained, low-phosphorus soil in full sun, giving it the room of a small specimen tree rather than a shrub border.

directions: Waboom, or Wagon Tree, is the only Protea species that reliably grows into a true small tree, with broad gray-green leaves and cream-to-pink flowerheads borne through the cooler months. Its common name comes from its historic use in South Africa, where the dense, durable wood was once favored for wagon wheels and its tannin-rich bark used in leather tanning. Unlike most of its fire-killed relatives, Waboom is protected by thick, corky bark and typically resprouts after wildfire rather than depending solely on seed regeneration. Plant it in full sun in sharply drained, low-phosphorus soil and allow it the room of a small specimen tree rather than a shrub border.
